accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS ELA Language L.3.1e ('Form and use the simple (e.g., I walked; I walk; I will walk) verb tenses') and L.3.1d, the DfE 2013 English programme of study (Year 2 consistent present and past tense) and its glossary note that English has no future tense inflection and treats will as a modal; the lesson says so in the adult text and labels will + verb 'future' only as the US standard does. Third-person spelling rules (add s; es after ch, sh, s, x, z; consonant + y to ies; vowel + y keeps y: plays) were checked in the Cambridge Grammar of English and the DfE Appendix 1 spelling rules (Y1 -s/-es). Every lab tile was checked by hand: walked/walks/will walk, went/goes/will go, tried/tries/will try, fetches, carries, lies.

misconceptions.evidence: The documented Year 3 slips are each targeted: s or ed after will (step 3 prediction 'will goes' vs 'will go'; tiles will walks, will swam, will went, will reading each with its own message), dropping or misspelling the third-person ending (step 2 prediction 'carrys' vs 'carries'; feedback for none vs s, es after ch/sh/x/z, ies for consonant + y, s for vowel + y), reading the simple present as 'only right now' (step 1 prediction about Every Monday), and tense drift (step 5 future plan with 'ate' and 'drives', challenge 'Yesterday she walks … bought').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagwill is built on the three simple tenses and their markers: a three-bin time-clue sort, a he/she/it ending picker with four ending tiles (none, +s, +es, +ies), a will + verb gap with distractors that add s, ed or -ing after will, a 3×3 tense table filled one tile at a time by row (verb) and column (time), a future plan with two drifting verbs, and a word-chip builder that rewrites I walk to school for yesterday, every day and tomorrow. flagtense (411) is a past/present timeline with -ed spelling and the progressive helper; no flagship lab uses will, the third-person spelling rules or a tense table. The lab_distinct gate passed under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner meets each rule by doing: the ending tiles show the prompt 'One person or thing: he, she or it' or 'Not he, she or it', and a wrong tile returns the specific spelling rule; the will gap rejects will walks and will walked with 'After will, no s' and 'walked is past'; the tense table only accepts a tile in the right verb row and time column and says which part was wrong; the rebuild step keeps every word but the verb, so the child sees that only the verb changes across the three times.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each hold a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: 'only right now' for Every Monday (the clue sort files every Saturday, usually and always as present habits), 'carrys' (the ending step turns carry into carries via consonant + y), and 'will goes' (every will tile with s is rejected). The completion line names the learner's own pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions; each wrong option carries its own tag and message: 'past' (that is the past, check the clue), 'willed' (after will use the plain verb), 'wills' (the verb after will never takes s), 'y' (consonant then y: change y to i, add es), 'noend' (the baby is one person, add an ending), 'future' (yesterday means it is over), 'keep' (walks is present but the rest is past) and 'es' (search ends in ch, add es).

readability.evidence: Measured kid FK grade 1.4 (limit 5.0 for family lessons) and adult 5.0 (limit 10.0) with learn/readability.py after splitting the long adult sentences. Kid paragraphs give one rule per sentence with an example (She will swim. Never add s or ed after will.). The terms modal, bare infinitive and progressive appear only in the adult text; on 360 px screenshots the lab headers stay one line.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid sentence states a rule or a clue word; the adult text gives the US and England requirements, the three forms with their spelling rules, the habit vs right-now distinction, named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler phrases, and the explanation is under 12% the same as every other lesson, including Past, Present and Progressive Tense (411) and Standard English verbs (792).

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark for all seven steps: the clue card is 52 px tall over three bins, the four ending tiles fit one row ('no ending' was shortened to 'none' after the first screenshot squeezed it), the three will tiles fit one row, the 3×3 table has 54 px cells with readable 14 px words, the 21-word plan wraps into four rows of tiles, and the sentence chips wrap into two rows. The browser walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button below: Past/Present/Future with the clue in the aria-label, the four endings with the subject and verb, each will option read as the full sentence, nine table buttons named by verb and time, one button per word in the plan, and one per sentence chip. Tapping a bin or table cell also places the card. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action, challenge feedback is a role=status live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme on desktop and iPhone 13.
